1.x: “And Jesus answered..”: Jesus is responding to the chief priests and Pharisees who sought to arrest him after his previous parables (Mt 21:45-46). He continues to speak aggressively using parabolic hidden truth.

2.x: “...a certain king..”: The King represents God the Father (YHWH, the divine Spirit, Holy Spirit, God). “... a marriage for His Son”: The Son is the man Jesus Christ (1 Tim 2:5) in whom the Father dwelt (Col 2:9-10; 2 Cor 5:19). The marriage represents the ultimate, joyful consummation of God’s redemptive plan: the wedding of the Messiah (God in the flesh) to His covenant people (“Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready” - Rev 19:7 KJV).

3.x: “..sent forth his servants to call them that were bidden..”: In ancient Near Eastern custom, a double invitation was given. The guests were “bidden” long in advance, and then when the feast was finally ready, servants were dispatched to announce that it was time to come. The “bidden” guests are the nation of Israel. The first wave of servants represents the OT prophets and John the Baptist. “..and they would not come”: This describes Israel’s general apathy and historical rejection of God’s prophetic warnings.

4.x: “..other servants..” This second wave of servants represents the apostles and early disciples preaching the gospel after the resurrection. “..all things are ready..”: The ultimate sacrifice has been made; Christ has died and risen. The meal is fully prepared; salvation is accomplished.

5.x: “But they made light of it..”: They treated the King’s ultimate invitation with utter contempt, indifference, and triviality(as something unimportant or insignificant). “..one to his farm, another to his merchandise:” They prioritized earthly gain, material wealth, and daily business over eternal salvation.

6.x: “..took his servants.. And slew them”: This shifts from indifference to violent hostility. This was historically fulfilled in the book of Acts with the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7), the execution of James “the great” (Acts 12), and the systemic persecution of the early church by Jewish religious authorities.

7.x: “..he sent forth his armies.. And burned up their city”: This is a direct, staggering prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem in 70AC. God utilized the Roman legions under Titus as His providential instrument (“His armies”) to execute national judgement on the city that rejected His Son.

8.x: “..they which were bidden were not worthy”: By rejecting the gospel, Israel judged themselves unworthy of everlasting life: “Then Paul and Barnabas waxed bold, and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.” (Acts 13:46 KJV).

9.x: “Go ye therefore into the highways..”: Because the original guests refused, the invitation was thrown open to the global streets. This represents the Gentile Commission, the spreading of the gospel outside Judea to all nations.

10.x: “..both bad and good..”: The gospel call goes out indiscriminately to all moral categories. Outcasts, sinners, and the unrighteous are gathered into the visible church today.

11.x: “...when the king came in to see the guests…”: This represents the final, scrutinizing judgement of God. “...a man which had not on a wedding garment”: In eastern royal banquets, the host king would traditionally provide appropriate festive garments at the door for all attendees. All guests were rounded up hastily from “the roads” and therefore none could be expected to come with proper attire. That means the wedding garments were supplied by the King Himself. So anyone lacking proper garment indicates he had rejected the King’s own gracious provision. To refuse the provided robe and insist on sitting at the royal table in one’s own filthy, everyday rags was a profound insult to the monarch. This represents coming to God with your own “goodness” and “good works” that are like “filthy rags” before a Holy God (Isa 64:6) instead of “putting on Christ” at baptism (Gal 3:27) and accepting his righteousness. The imagery shows those who identify with the kingdom externally, profess to be Christians, belong to the church in a visible sense, yet spurn the garment of righteousness Christ offers by seeking to establish a righteousness of their own. Ashamed to admit their own spiritual poverty, they refuse the better garment the King graciously offers, and thus they are guilty of a horrible sin against God.

12.x: “Friend..”: A term used ironically (similar to how Jesus addresses Judas in the garden). “..And he was speechless”: The man had no excuse. He cannot claim he was too poor to afford a garment, because the King provided them freely. His nakedness is a deliberate choice of self-will. Facing divine judgement, the hypocrite is stripped of all self-justification.

13.x: "...cast him into outer darkness..." This is standard biblical terminology for Hell and eternal damnation. The wedding feast is full of light and warmth; to be cast outside is to experience permanent, agonizing separation from God.

14.x: "For many are called..." The general invitation of the Gospel goes out globally to all people who hear the preaching of the Word. "...but few are chosen." Only those who genuinely respond in faith, submit to the terms of the King, and allow themselves to be clothed in the righteousness of Christ rather than their own works are ultimately sealed for eternity.

The "wedding garment" represents the essential robe of righteousness that must be applied to a believer's life before they can sit at the table of the King. Scripture identifies exactly how this garment is obtained: (1) Imputed Righteousness through Baptism: In Galatians 3:27, Paul explicitly uses the garment metaphor: "For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have PUT ON CHRIST." The wedding garment is not manufactured by human good works; it is the uniform of the King applied when a believer submits to water baptism in the Name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins (Acts 2:38). (2) The Robe of Holiness: In Revelation 19:8, the Lamb's wife is permitted to be arrayed in "fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints." The garment implies a transformed life. You cannot enter the kingdom while clinging to your old lifestyle of sin. The man without the garment represents the religious hypocrite or the self-righteous legalist, someone who wants the benefits of the King's table (Heaven) but refuses to submit to the King's terms of salvation. We are saved by faith, but a faith that keeps us swimming, not a mere intellectual assent. Examples of having faith that does not save: (1) Simon Magus: He believed, got baptized, yet Peter says he needs to repent (Acts 8:21-23). (2) Many who believed during Jesus’ ministry: “many BELIEVED in his name, when they saw the miracles which he did. But Jesus did not commit himself unto them... because he knew all men” (Jn 2:23-25 KJV) - a real saving faith will always produce eternal fruit. (3) Temporary Believers: Jesus describes people who initially believe but later fall away: "They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away." (Lk 8:13 KJV). (4) Many Chief Rulers: "Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him...For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God” (Jn 12:42-43 KJV). (5) Judas Iscariot: The 12th apostle that followed Jesus for years and even participated in his ministry, yet Jesus declared him lost: "...none of them is lost, but the son of perdition..." (Jn 17:12 KJV). (6) Those who call him “Lord”: "Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven...And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, YE THAT WORK INIQUITY(the real reason why they were not saved, their faith did not produce real fruit)" (Mt 7:21-23 KJV). (7) Demons: "Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble." (Jms 2:19 KJV). We are not saved by works, but a real faith will always have works: “Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone” (Jms 2:17 KJV) - and notice how what’s always being tested for salvation is the faith, not the works. The works are evidence of a real saving faith.

15.x: Following the Parable of the Wedding Feast, Jesus’ opponents realize he is painting them as rebels facing imminent divine judgement. Rather than repenting, they form an unprecedented political alliance to trap him in a public dilemma that will either lead to his execution by Rome or ruin his reputation with the Jewish crowds. “Then went the Pharisees…”: The Pharisees were the conservatives, anti-Roman religious purists of Jewish society. “..how they might entangle him..”: The Greek word “pagideuo” means to set a snare or trap, like a hunter catching a wild animal. They are intentionally engineering a lose-lose scenario.

16.x: “...with the Herodians…”: This details a hypocritical alliance. The Herodians were a secular, political faction that supported the Roman-appointed dynasty of Herod and favored complete cooperation with Rome. Normally, the Pharisees and Herodians despised each other. Yet, their mutual hatred for Jesus unites them. “...Master, we know that thou art true…”: They unleash toxic flattery to disarm him. They praise him for being courageous and impartial (“neither carest thou for any man”), hoping to egg him into making a bold, reckless political statement.

17.x: “...Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not?”: This is the trap. The “tribute”(kensos) was the Roman poll tax, a deeply detested annual tax levied on every individual in Judea, requiring payment in Roman currency. If Jesus answers YES, the Jewish multitudes will instantly abandon him. They view paying the tax as submission to a pagan oppressor and treason against God(YHWH), the true King of Israel. If Jesus answers NO, the Herodians will immediately report him to Pontius Pilate as a seditious revolutionary inciting a tax revolt against Rome, which carried an automatic death penalty.

18.x: “But Jesus perceived their wickedness..”: Recall that Jesus sometimes speaks as the human Son, and sometimes as the eternal Father. This Jesus most likely refers to the human Son, as you don’t need the Father’s omniscience to realize they’re being hypocritical. “..Why tempt ye me, ye hypocrites?”: He confronts them bluntly. By calling them hypocrites, he exposes the fraud of their flattering introduction; they pretend to be sincere students of the law, but they are actually acting as religious assassins.

19.x: “Shew me the tribute money”: Jesus takes control of the situation. He doesn’t just talk; he creates an interactive object lesson. “..And they brought unto him a penny”: The “penny” refers to a Roman silver denarius. By physically pulling this coin out of their pocket inside the temple precincts, the Pharisees reveal their own hypocrisy: they are actively carrying and profiting from the very Roman currency they pretend to religiously despise.

20.x: “..Whose is this image and superscription?”: Jesus forces them to describe the coin. The coin bore the stamped profile image of Tiberius Caesar. The “superscription” (engraving) read: TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS (“Tiberius Caesar, Son of the Divine Augustus”). To strict Jews, carrying an image claiming a human ruler was “divine” was a direct violation of the 2nd Commandment against graven images (Exo 20:4-5).

21.x: “They say unto him, Caesar’s”: They answer their own trap. “Render therefore unto Caesar..”: The word “render” (apodidomi) means to pay back a debt or return something to its rightful owner. Jesus argues that because Caesar’s name and face are stamped on the silver, the physical coin belongs to his earthly economy. Paying taxes is simply returning to Caesar what already belongs to him. Christians have a civil obligation to obey government authority, pay taxes, and maintain social order (a principle Paul confirms in Romans 13:1-7). “...and unto God the things that are God’s”: This is the masterstroke. If the coin belongs to Caesar because it bears Caesar’s image, human beings belong to God because they bear God’s image (Gen 1:27). Caesar can have his silver, but he cannot have your soul, your worship, or your absolute allegiance. That territory belongs strictly to the Creator.

22.x: “..they marvelled, and left him..”: The trap is completely broken. Jesus did not compromise his loyalty to God, nor did he break Roman law. He managed to elevate the conversation from a petty political trap into a profound theological truth about human identity and divine ownership. Dumbfounded, the conspirators retreat in total defeat.

23.x: Immediately after Jesus silences the Pharisees, the Sadducees step forward to launch their own assault. The Sadducees were the wealthy, aristocratic priestly class of Israel. Politically, they collaborated with Rome, and ideologically, they were strict rationalists who rejected the supernatural, including angels, spirits, and the resurrection of the dead. They present Jesus with a highly exaggerated, hypothetical scenario designed to make the doctrine of the resurrection look logically absurd. “The same day..”: The attacks are relentless. As soon as one faction retreats, the next advances in the temple courts. “..which say that there is no resurrection…”: This is the core theological dividing line. Because the Sadducees only accepted the five books of Moses (the Torah) as fully authoritative, they claimed the doctrine of a future physical resurrection could not be found in scripture.

Matthes 22:24: “..Moses said..”: They appeal directly to the Torah (Deut 25:5-6), citing the law of Levirate marriage. If a married man died childless, his brother was legally obligated to marry the widow. The firstborn son of that new union would carry on the deceased brother’s name and inherit his property, ensuring that families did not die out and land stayed within the tribe.

28.x: “..whose wife shall she be of the seven?”: This is their supposed checkmate. They reason that if the resurrection is real, eternity will be plagued by messy, polyandrous marital chaos in heaven. They are trying to force Jesus to either deny Moses’ marriage law or admit that the resurrection creates a ridiculous moral contradiction.

29.x: “Ye do err..”: Jesus diagnoses their theological failure completely. The root of their heresy is not intellectual superiority, but profound spiritual ignorance. “..not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God”: This double indictment targets their two main blind spots: (1) They do not understand the true depth of the written Word of God; (2) They possess a shrunken view of God’s power, assuming that the Almighty cannot create a heavenly reality that transcends basic human biology. In this verse, Jesus lays down a universal principle regarding how he expects human beings to interact with divine truth. His rebuke: “Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures,” demonstrates that God holds us completely accountable for our knowledge (or lack thereof) of His Word. Jesus expects our engagement with scripture to be characterized by three distinct markers: (1) Ignorance of Scripture is the Root of Moral and Doctrinal Error: Jesus does not treat theological error as a harmless difference of opinion. He says: “Ye do err, because you do not know…” When individuals, churches, or cultures drift into sin or false doctrine, it is always anchored in a failure to deeply know, study, and submit to the scriptures. We cannot live a life pleasing to God if we are ignorant of what God actually has spoken. (2) We Must Know the Whole Counsel of God, Not Just Our Favorite Parts: The Sadducees knew the letter of Deut 25, but they didn’t know the scriptures synthetically (“as a whole”, “complete structure”- meaning they did not understand how the parts fit together into one unified message). They read the Bible selectively, discarding everything outside the Torah and twisting Moses’ civil concessions to mock eternal realities. Jesus expects us to be comprehensive readers of the Word: interpreting specific laws in light of God’s overarching eternal character and context. (3) Scripture and Divine Power are Inseparable: Jesus links “the scriptures” with “the power of God.” To know the Word correctly is to understand that God is not bound by the limitations of human logic, physical death, or earthly biology. When we study the scriptures with faith, we are introduced to an omnipotent God who can raise the dead and completely transform human existence. This is why so many people are transformed instantly the moment they read the Word of God and believe in it.

30.x: “..they neither marry, nor are given in marriage..”: Jesus shatters their false premise. Earthly marriage was instituted by God at creation for companionship and the propagation of the human race. In the resurrection, death is completely conquered; therefore, procreation is no longer necessary, and the temporary earthly institution of marriage is superseded by a far greater, universal spiritual unity with God. “..but are as the angels of God in heaven”: Notice Jesus specifically validates the existence of angels, subtly rebuking another core Sadducean error (Acts 23:8) while clarifying that resurrected humans will share the non-marrying, immortal nature of the angelic realm.

31.x: “But as touching the resurrection..”: Jesus shifts from defensive explanation to an aggressive scriptural counter-offensive. “...have ye not read that which was spoken unto you by God”: Notice Christ’s phrasing. Even though these words were written by Moses in a scroll centuries prior, Jesus says God(YHWH, the Father, the Holy Spirit) spoke these Words “unto you.” Jesus(the man born of Mary in whom the omnipresent Spirit of God dwells) views the written scripture as a living, direct communication from God to the present reader.

32.x: “I am the God of Abraham…”: Jesus quotes Exodus 3:6, the account of God speaking to Moses from the burning bush. This is a brilliant strategic move. Because the Sadducees only accepted the Torah (the first five books of Moses), Jesus bypasses obvious resurrection passages in the Prophets (like Daniel 12:2 or Isaiah 26:19) and finds the resurrection hidden right inside the books they claimed to revere. Jesus bases his theological proof on the PRESENT TENSE of an implied verb. When God spoke to Moses, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had been physically dead and buried for hundreds of years. Yet, God did not say: “I WAS the God of your fathers.” He said: “I AM (present tense) the God of Abraham.” “...God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.”: If Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had completely ceased to exist at physical death, God would be calling Himself the ruler of non-existent corpses. Because God maintains a present-tense covenant relationship with them, they must still exist in the spiritual realm, safely awaiting the future physical resurrection of their bodies.

From a Oneness point of view, when God speaks at the burning bush in Exodus 3, He identifies Himself as a singular, undivided Divine Ego: “I AM.” He does not reveal Himself as a plurality of persons, a committee, or a multi-personal Godhead. The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is one identical Divine Spirit - the same Spirit that later manifested in the flesh as Jesus Christ. In John 8:58, Jesus explicitly claimed that identical title for Himself (“Before Abraham was, I AM”). Therefore, when Jesus tells the Sadducees what God means in Exodus 3:6, he is not merely offering an astute human interpretation; He is the same God in the flesh that said: “I AM has sent me to you” (Ex 3:14 KJV) explaining His own original intent to His creation. For Trinitarians, the God that made Himself manifested in the burning bush to Moses is God-the-Son, the pre-incarnate Christ, the Logos of the Father. Meaning, there is still another God-the-Father up in heaven, while only God-the-Son interacted with humans. This understanding comes from Hellenistic culture where the Supreme God of the philosophers was so Holy that He could not be named, He could not be personal, and He could not interact with Humanity; so early Christian Philosophers, like Justin Martyr(~150AC), equated this Supreme God of the Greek philosophers with God-the-Father, making Christianity more digestible to the pagan audiences. And to solve the issue of the Supreme God not being personal, Christian philosophers came up with the Logos doctrine, where only His Logos(“Word”) could come and interact with people, but not the Supreme God (God-the-Father). At this point in history, these Christian philosophers taught subordinationism: that God-the-Father is greater and more powerful than God-the-Son (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen, all taught a form of subordinationism). It would take centuries to tune up the final doctrine of the Trinity (for example, the filoque, the statement that the Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son, wasn’t added to the official definition of the Trinity until 589AC in a local council of Spain, and it would take even more years for Rome to adopt this change. The Eastern Orthodox never accepted this change).

Roman Catholics often use Matthew 22:32 (“God is not the God of the dead, but of the living”) to build their defense for the Catholic practice of praying to deceased saints. Their reasoning is that since Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are actually “living “ right now in heaven and part of the same “Body of Christ”, it is perfectly logical to ask them to pray and intercede on our behalf, just as we would ask a friend on earth to pray for us. However, this is totally contrary to the Scriptural pattern where prayer is only directed towards God and where the apostles and God Himself teach us to pray to them directly (Ps 50:15; 65:2; Jer 29:12; 33:3; Isa 55:6; Phil 4:6; Mt 6:9; Jn 16:23-24; 15:16, etc). So while it is true that departed saints are spiritually conscious and alive in the presence of God, using this passage to justify praying to them is completely invalid both scripturally and historically: (1) The Total Absence of Omniscience: The fundamental breakdown in the Catholic analogy (“asking a saint to pray for you is just like asking a friend on earth”) is a matter of basic physics and theology. If you ask a friend on earth to pray to you, they hear you because of spatial, physical proximity or communication lines. For a deceased saint in heaven (like Mary or Peter) TO HEAR MILLIONS OF DISTINCT, SILENT, MENTAL PRAYERS WHISPERED SIMULTANEOUSLY BY PEOPLE ALL OVER THE GLOBE IN DIFFERENT LANGUAGES, that saint would have to possess OMNISCIENCE (the ability to know all things) and OMNIPRESENCE(the ability to be everywhere at once). Scripture teaches that these are incommunicable attributes belonging strictly to God alone (1 Jn 3:20; Ps 147:5; Heb 4:13; Ps 139:7-10; 1 Kings 8:27). Even Angels are limited, in Daniel 9:21-23, the angel Gabriel flies to Daniel after being sent. In Luke 1:26, Gabriel is sent from God to Nazareth. In Matthew 24:36, the Angels do not know the hour of the second coming of Jesus. There is no one like God (Isa 40:25; 46:5), God’s unique attributes set Him apart from every created being. By directing prayers to saints, the Catholic system inadvertently attributes divinity to human beings. (2) Direct Violation of the One Mediator Rule: the Bible explicitly outlines the exact pathway for all human prayer, completely cutting out any third-party human mediators in the spiritual realm: “For there is one God, and ONE MEDIATOR BETWEEN GOD AND MEN, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). Jesus did not tell us to pray to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, or Mary. He commanded us to go directly to the Father in his name: “Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father IN MY NAME, He will give it you” (Jn 16:23). Attempting to route prayers through deceased believers implies that Jesus is either too unapproachable or insufficient as our high priest, directly undermining his unique mediatorial role. (3) Biblical Prohibition Against Communicating with the Dead: Scripture draws a severe, impenetrable boundary line between the living on earth and the dead in the spiritual realm. Attempting to initiate contact, talk to, or petition individuals who have passed away falls under the biblical definition of NECROMANCY or SPIRITISM, which is strictly condemned throughout God’s Word: "There shall not be found among you any one... that useth divination... Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer [one who calls upon the dead]" (Deut 18:10–11, KJV). While Abraham is alive to God in the spiritual economy, he is dead to this world. We are forbidden from attempting to cross that boundary to establish communication. A perfect example is King Saul, the Bible explicitly states that one of the reasons Saul died was because HE CONSULTED A MEDIUM TO INQUIRE OF THE DEAD (a dead Saint: Samuel) instead of seeking the LORD (1 Sam 28:6-7; 13-15; 1 Chr 10:13-14). Notice Saul could not simply “pray” to dead Samuel, he had to use a medium to summon him in order to be able to talk to him. (4) The Historical Reality: A Pagan Intrusion: Historically, the early Apostolic church NEVER PRAYED TO SAINTS. You cannot find a single instance of an apostle or first-century believer praying to a deceased believer in the NT or in the earliest records of the church (such as the writings of Clement of Rome or Polycarp). The practice of praying to saints didn’t systematically develop until the late 3rd and 4th centuries. As massive numbers of Roman pagans flooded into the institutionalized church after the conversion of Emperor Constantine, they brought their old polytheistic habits with them. In paganism, people were accustomed to praying to specific localized deities or demigos who patronized different professions or problems (“god of agriculture”, “god of the sea”, “god of thunder”, “god of lost things”, etc). The institutional church accommodated this by simply REPLACING THE PAGAN DEMIGOS WITH CHRISTIAN “SAINTS”, turning the goddess of sailors into a saint for sailors, and turning prayers to dead ancestors into prayers to Christian martyrs. It is a historical corruption of the primitive, apostolic faith.

33.x: “..they were astonished at his doctrine”: The crowds are utterly stunned. For generations, the brilliant Sadducees had used their marriage riddle to embarrass opponents. Jesus completely dismantles their entire theological framework with a single present-tense verb from a familiar passage of scripture.

34.x: “..heard that he had put the Sadducees to silence..”: The Greek word for “silence” is “phimoo,” which literally means to muzzle or gag. Jesus had completely shut down the Sadducees’ theological argument. “..they were gathered together”: While the Pharisees were glad their theological rivals were embarrassed, they were terrified of Jesus’ rising authority. They regroup to form a unified front.

35.x: “..a lawyer”: This does not mean a secular attorney; in first-century Israel, a lawyer(nomikos) was an expert scholar in the divine jurisprudence of the Mosaic Law and the oral traditions. “...tempting him..”: Like the previous group, this scribe is trying to push Jesus into a controversial corner.

36.x: “..which is the great commandment in the law?”: Jewish theologians of the day had cataloged 613 distinct commandments in the Torah (365 negative prohibitions and 248 positive injunctions). They fiercely debated which laws were “heavy” (weighty and essential) and which were “light” (less critical). They wanted to see if Jesus would elevate one specific law at the expense of others, which would allow them to accuse him of diminishing the rest of God’s Word.

37.x: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God..”: Jesus quoted the Shema (Deut 6:5), the foundational daily declaration of monotheistic Israel. “..with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind”: True love for God is not an erratic emotional feeling; it demands the total, integrated devotion of the entire human being: (1) Heart (kardia): The center of the will, desires, and affections; (2) Soul (psyche): The seat of life, breath, and conscious existence; (3) Mind (dianoia): The faculty of understanding, intellect, and deliberate thought. God does not accept divided loyalties. He demands the absolute, undivided allegiance of our entire internal and external life.

38.x: “This is the first..”: It is first in priority, first in chronology, and first in dignity. Every other commandment is entirely secondary to, and dependent upon, our foundational relationship with the Creator.

39.x: “And the second is like unto it..”: Jesus doesn’t wait for a follow-up question. He immediately provides a second commandment because the first cannot exist without it. It is “like unto it” - possessing the exact same divine authority and moral weight. “..Thous shalt love thy neighbor as thyself”: Jesus quotes Lev 19:18. True vertical love for God must manifest horizontally as love for other human beings. You cannot claim to revere the invisible Creator while simultaneously mistreating or despising the visible human beings who are stamped in His unique image (John specifically addresses this in: 1 Jn 4:20).

40.x: “On these two commandments hang…”: The Greek word is “kremannymi”, meaning to suspend from a peg or hook. Jesus uses a brilliant visual metaphor. If you remove the anchor hook, the entire garment falls to the floor. Similarly, the 613 individual laws are not a random collection of arbitrary rules; they are specific, practical expressions of these two primary weights. For example, love for God requires a vertical relationship described in the first 4 commandments of the decalogue (no other gods, no graven images, honor his name, keep the Sabbath), while love for neighbor requires a horizontal relationship described in commandments 5-10 of the decalogue (honor parents, do not murder, commit adultery, steal, lie, or covet). “...all the law and the prophets”: This phrase encompasses the entirety of the OT scriptures. Jesus teaches that the ultimate goal of all divine revelation, all prophetic warning, and all legal boundaries is simply to produce a people who love God completely and love their fellow man unselfishly.

43.x: “..How then doth David in Spirit..”: Jesus notes that David was writing under the direct, divine inspiration of the Holy Spirit (“in spirit”). “..call him Lord..”: Jesus highlights a profound relational anomaly. In the patriarchal culture of the ancient Near East, a father or ancestor was always superior to his son. A father would never call his own grandson or descendant “My Lord.” Yet, under divine inspiration, David explicitly subordinates himself to his future descendant.

44.x: “The LORD said unto my Lord..”: Jesus quotes Psalms 110:1. In the original Hebrew text, this reads “YHWH said unto my Lord(Adonai).” Meaning, the eternal God(YHWH) prophetically speaking to the human born of Mary(Jesus). This does not refer to two divine persons or to two YHWH’s, rather, it refers to one divine person (YHWH) glorifying His temple & visible image (human Jesus) to the position of privilege by giving the human the power and authority of the Father Himself. “..Sit thou on my right hand..”: Trinitarians view this verse as a conversation between two distinct divine persons who are co-equal, co-eternal: God-the-Father talking to God-the-Son. However, God is Spirit (Jn 4:24), hence He does not have a right or left side. The “right hand” in Scripture functions as a figure of speech for the place of highest honor, authority, strength, protection, or favor, rather than describing God’s physical anatomy. God is Spirit so He is not confined to a physical form. Scripture teaches us what the “right hand” means: (1) The “right hand” is a place of honor: In ancient Israel, the person seated at a king’s right hand occupied the position of greatest honor and delegated authority. A clear OT example is: "Bathsheba therefore went unto king Solomon... and the king rose up to meet her... and caused a seat to be set for the king's mother; and SHE SAT ON HIS RIGHT HAND” (1 Kings 2:19 KJV) - Bathsheba was not literally part of Solomon’s body. Sitting at his right hand signified her honored position. Likewise: “..upon THY RIGHT HAND did stand the queen in gold of Ophir” (Ps 45:9 KJV) - Again, the right side is the place of honor. (2) Jesus at the right hand of God: After his resurrection, Jesus is repeatedly said to sit at God’s right hand: "Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on THE RIGHT HAND OF POWER, and coming in the clouds of heaven." (Mk 26:64 KJV). Notice Jesus does not say “the right hand of God.” He says: “the right hand OF POWER.” Here, “Power” is a reverential way of referring to God. The phrase emphasizes the glorified human sharing God’s kingly authority, not occupying one side of a divine body. (3) The man Jesus reigns with God’s authority: "...when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on THE RIGHT HAND OF THE MAJESTY on high." (Heb 1:3 KJV) - notice the expression: “the right hand of the Majesty”. The emphasis is on royal majesty and authority. Likewise: "Which he wrought in Christ... and set him at HIS OWN RIGHT HAND in the heavenly places, Far above all principality, and power, and might..." - and Paul immediately explains what “right hand” means: Christ has been exalted above every authority. (4) Stephen’s vision: "...he... saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God." (Acts 7:55-56 KJV) - Stephen sees Jesus in the position of exaltation by God, he sees glorified Jesus, that’s why Stephen only acknowledges and prays to Jesus, the only visible body: “they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59 KJV). 1 Tim 6:16 teaches that God dwells in light “whom no man hath seen, NOR CAN SEE,” but the man Jesus, being the image of the invisible Spirit, is the one we see when we see God, so the vision communicates Christ’s exalted status rather than two divine bodies next to each other on a literal “right hand.” (5) God is at David’s right hand: One of the strongest examples that “right hand” is idiomatic is that God Himself is said to be at a human’s right hand: "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved." (Ps 16:8 KJV) - Is God literally standing on David’s physical right side at all times? The meaning is that God is David’s protector and helper. (6) God is at the right hand of the poor: An even clearer example: "For he shall stand at the right hand of the poor, to save him from those that condemn his soul." (Ps 109:31 KJV) - Again, this describes God’s protection and advocacy, not His physical location. (7) God’s right hand represents His power: “Thy right hand, O LORD, is become glorious in power” (Ex 15:6 KJV) & “The right hand of the LORD is exalted: the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly” (Ps 118:16 KJV) - these are poetic expressions for God’s saving strength. Isaiah likewise says: “..I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness” (Isa 41:10 KJV) - God is not describing a physical hand but His faithful, powerful support. (8) The Messiah is God’s right hand: The Messiah (human Jesus) is described as God’s right hand: “Let thy hand be upon THE MAN OF THY RIGHT HAND, upon THE SON OF MAN whom thou madest strong for thyself” (Ps 80:17 KJV) - this is another example where “right hand” denotes God’s chose and exalted representative on Earth. (9) God does not have a physical body: The Bible repeatedly teaches that God(YHWH, the Father, the Holy Spirit) transcends physical limitations: “God is a Spirit..” (Jn 4:24 KJV); “Now unto the King eternal, immortal, INVISIBLE…” (1 Tim 1:17 KJV); “..whom no man hath seen, nor can see..” (1 Tim 6:16 KJV). These passages caution against reading anthropomorphic expression (hand, eyes, arm, face, etc) as describing God’s literal physical form. Scripture uses human language to communicate God’s actions and relationship with HIs people, so a Trinitarian view of one divine person physically sitting next to another divine person is terribly misguided. The biblical evidence shows that “the right hand” is an idiom for supreme honor, authority, favor, strength, and protection, so when the Lord sits at the right hand of the LORD(YHWH), it is a primarily theological and royal metaphor, conveying shared authority, honor, power, protection, and favor: aka the glorified human Messiah after resurrection. In conclusion, the phrase “The LORD(YHWH) said unto my Lord” from Psalm 110:1 is a prophetic look forward to the incarnation. It describes the eternal Spirit (YHWH) conferring absolute authority and dominion upon the human manifestation (the Son). Because God chose to manifest Himself in human form to die for our sins, that human body (the Son) had to be elevated to the position of supreme power. The “right hand” simply means that the humanity of Jesus was clothed with the full, unrestricted power of the invisible Godhead. As Paul states in Colossians 2:9: “For in him dwelleth ALL the fulness of the Godhead bodily.”

45.x: “If David then call him Lord, how is he his son?”: This is Christ’s ultimate checkmate. He poses a riddle that first-century Jewish theology could not solve: How can the Messiah be both David’s superior (his Lord) and David’s inferior (his physical son) at the same time? Jesus here demonstrates that God is truly the first (the root) and the last (the descendant of David). In the OT, YHWH alone declares Himself to the “the First and the Last” (Isa 44:6). The human Jesus applies the same title to himself because he is the same YHWH of the OT come in the flesh: “Fear not; I am the first and the last: I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore..” (Rev 1:17-18 KJV). The eternal one became a man (Jn 1:1,14), the one who existed before creation entered human history through the virgin birth.God Himself accomplished redemption through His human Messiah: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV). Throughout Isaiah, YHWH repeatedly says that HE ALONE is Israel’s singular Savior: “I, even I, am the LORD(YHWH); and beside me there is no saviour” (Isa 43:11 KJV) & “..there is no God else beside me; a just God and a Saviour; there is none beside me. Look unto me, and be ye saved…” (Isa 45:21-22 KJV). Yet the NT declares that salvation comes through Jesus: “..thou shalt call his name JESUS(which means YWHW-saves): for he shall SAVE his people from their sins” (Mt 1:21 KJV) as “Immanuel, which is translated ‘God(YHWH) with us’ ”(Mt 1:23 KJV) & “Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13 KJV). That’s why Luke can say that God purchased the Church “with His own blood” (Acts 20:28 KJV), because He was one with the human Jesus (Jn 10:30). God does not have blood according to His divine nature, yet the One who is God took on a human vessel (His own human Son) and shed His blood for the Church (***notice that even respected Trinitarians like McArthur write: “Paul believed so strongly in the unity of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ that he could speak of Christ’s death as shedding the blood of God- who has no body and hence no blood” [Study notes on McArthur Study Bible for Acts 20:28]). Also, the Redeemer is YHWH: “Thus saith the LORD(YHWH), thy redeemer..” (Isa 44:24 KJV). Yet the NT identifies Jesus as the Redeemer: “In whom we have REDEMPTION through his blood..” (Eph 1:7 KJV). So as the FIRST, He is the eternal YHWH who existed before all creation. In the fullness of time, He became veiled by humanity through Mary without ceasing to be who He eternally is. As the LAST, He completed the work of redemption through His death and resurrection and now reigns forever as the risen exalted Messiah. The same divine person who is eternally “the First and the Last” is the One who says: “I was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore” (Rev 1:17-18). Only God could be both the Root and Descendant of David (Rev 22:16), only God could be both the Sacrificial Lamb and the High Priest (Jn 1:29; Heb 4:14); and only God could be both the eternal divine Spirit, and the human person born of Mary: the First and the Last.

46.x: “And no man was able to answer him..”: The Pharisees are completely silenced. They lacked the theological categories to reconcile these two realities. “..neither durst any man.. ask him any more questions”: This brings the public cross-examination of Passion Week to a definitive end. Jesus has asserted his absolute intellectual and divine supremacy over the entire religious establishment (Pharisees, Sadducees, Herodians).

25-27.x: “Now there were with us seven brethren..”: They construct an extreme, comical, hypothetical scenario. One by one, seven brothers marry the exact same woman, and each brother dies childless. Finally, the woman dies.

41-42.x: Having systematically muzzled the Herodians, Sadducees, and the specialized Pharisaic lawyer, Jesus now takes the offensive. While the Pharisees are still gathered together in the temple courts, Jesus asks them a single question regarding the identity of the Messiah. “What think ye of Christ? Whose son is he?”: Jesus forces them to define the biological and covenantal lineage of the Messiah (Christos). “They say unto him, The Son of David”: The Pharisees give the standard, correct theological answer based on OT prophecies (like 2 Sam 7 and Isa 11:1). They knew the Messiah would be a physical descendant of King David’s royal line. However, their understanding was incomplete; they viewed the coming Messiah merely as a great human king, a political liberator, and an earthly successor to David’s throne.
